To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the placenta and the maternal liver of mice incorporate leucine- ^{14} C into proteins at different rates and that the pattern of incorporation of leucine into hepatic proteins differs between pregnant and nongraved animals.
the incorporation of leucine -14C into proteins of the liver of mice is higher during pregnancy than in nonpregnant mice.

the incorporation of leucine into placental and maternal liver protein is highest on the 15th day of gestation, and that the pattern of leucin incorporation into hepatic protein is different in the gravid and nongraivd animals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis of the placenta proteins in the mouse.
the synthesis of proteins in the liver of the gravid and nongravida mouse.
the study of protein metabolism in the placenta and in the liver during gestation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the placenta of the pregnant mouse is a tissue with a high capacity for amino acid incorporation.

leucine- ^{14} C was incorporated into placental and liver proteins of mice at a rate which varied as a function of gestation and that the rate of incorporation was different in the placenta and in the maternal liver of mice.
the pattern of leucination of placental and hepatic proteins in the gravid mouse is not the same as in the nongravid animal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
placenta and liver have different patterns of protein synthesis and that the patterns of placental protein synthesis are different in gravid and nongravide mice.
the incorporation of amino acids into proteins of the liver and placenta of mice differs as a function of the physiological state of the animals and the time of pregnancy.

leucine is incorporated into placental proteins at a rate greater than into maternal liver proteins, but that the rate of incorporation into liver proteins is higher than in the liver of nonpregnant animals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the incorporation of leucine in proteins is not a linear process, but it follows a pattern of incorporation.
there are differences in the pattern of protein synthesis in the placenta and in the maternal liver of pregnant mice.
the placenta and fetal liver are not simply passive recipients of maternal amino acids, but rather are metabolically active and capable of regulating their own protein synthetic rates.
